problemText: For centuries, camel caravans crossed the Sahara carrying two goods in opposite directions, and that exchange funded the empires of the West African Sahel. Which description of that exchange is correct?
choices: Salt traveled south from Saharan mines while gold traveled north from West African goldfields
Gold traveled south from Saharan mines while salt traveled north from West African goldfields
Both gold and salt were mined in the Sahara and carried south to the savanna together
Silk traveled south from North Africa while ivory traveled north from the forest zone
hints: Ask which region actually had the mines for each good — a desert has salt beds, not goldfields.

problemText: Students often confuse the medieval Empire of Ghana (roughly 700 to 1200) with the modern nation that carries the same name. Which statement about the empire is accurate?
choices: It occupied the same Atlantic coastal territory as the modern country of Ghana
It was founded by the modern country of Ghana after that country gained independence in 1957
It stood in the Sahel, in the region of present-day Mali and Mauritania; the modern nation adopted the old name in 1957 as an honor
It was a North African state that controlled the Mediterranean end of the caravan routes
hints: The empire sat where the goldfields met the desert crossings — the modern nation lies hundreds of miles away on the Atlantic coast.

problemText: West African societies trained specialists who memorized genealogies, praise songs, and long epics such as the story of Sundiata, passing them down across generations and being held to accuracy by their communities. Who were these specialists?
choices: Askias — provincial governors who compiled the empire's written tax records
Griots — trained professional oral historians whose accounts historians cross-check against written sources such as the traveler Ibn Battuta
Ulama — North African judges who composed West African history from Cairo
Missionaries — European visitors who first wrote down the region's traditions in the 1800s
hints: The record was carried in trained memory, not on paper — and 'oral' does not mean 'unchecked.'

problemText: An Egyptian administrator in Cairo, writing about fifteen years after the visit of Mali's ruler Mansa Musa in 1324, described it roughly this way: 'He left no court officeholder without a gift of gold, and so much gold changed hands that its price in our markets fell and had not recovered.' Taking the observation as broadly accurate, which economic mechanism does it describe?
choices: A sudden, very large increase in the supply of a good pushed its price down in that market
A shortage of gold in Cairo drove merchants to bid its price up
Mali's ruler bought up Egyptian gold, leaving less of it available in the city
Egypt's rulers deliberately devalued their coinage in order to attract foreign traders
hints: Ask what happens to the price of anything when an enormous quantity of it arrives in one market at once.

problemText: Under Mali and then Songhai, Timbuktu supported mosque-schools such as Sankore, salaried teachers of law and astronomy, and large family-owned manuscript libraries; handwritten books were among the most profitable goods sold in its markets. Which relationship does this best illustrate?
choices: Islamic law obligated every trading city to found and fund a university
European missionaries carried literacy into the West African interior during the 1400s
Scholarship could take root only in cities that owned and worked their own goldfields
Revenue from taxing long-distance trade paid for full-time scholars, schools, and a commercial market in books
hints: Someone has to feed people who read for a living — trace where the money came from before it reached the library.

problemText: In 1591 a Moroccan force of a few thousand men crossed the Sahara and broke a far larger Songhai army at Tondibi. At that moment Songhai still had appointed provincial governors, standardized weights, functioning trade cities, and patronage of scholarship. Which conclusion does this evidence best support?
choices: Songhai had already disintegrated internally, so the battle merely confirmed a collapse that was complete
A wealthy, well-administered state can still be destroyed when an opponent arrives with a decisive weapons advantage — here, firearms and cannon
European colonial armies had begun partitioning the West African interior by the 1590s
The Sahara had dried out by 1591, ending caravan trade and starving the empire of revenue
hints: Compare what each side actually brought to the field: numbers on one side, gunpowder weapons on the other.
Test the other options against dates and evidence — European partition of the interior comes roughly three centuries later, and Songhai's administration was still operating when the invasion arrived.

problemText: The Indian Ocean has a wind system that blows from the northeast for part of the year and then reverses to blow from the southwest for the rest of it. What is this system called, and why did merchants depend on it?
choices: The trade winds — they blew steadily in a single direction all year, so no voyage ever had to wait
The doldrums — a windless belt that forced crews to row their cargo across
The monsoon — its seasonal reversal let a merchant sail out on one wind and return home on the other
The gulf stream — an ocean current that carried ships east and west regardless of the weather
hints: The advantage was predictability, not speed: a wind that turns around on a calendar lets you plan the trip home before you leave.

problemText: Kiswahili is a Bantu language, African in its grammar and structure, that absorbed a large layer of Arabic loanwords over centuries of trade contact. What does this pattern best indicate about Swahili coast society?
choices: African communities took on Arabic vocabulary and Islam through long trade contact while remaining African societies
Arab settlers replaced the coastal population and founded the port cities themselves
Kiswahili is a dialect of Arabic that was simply written in a local script
Arab armies conquered the coast and imposed their language on the population by decree
hints: Look at what the language is underneath the borrowed words — grammar changes far more slowly than vocabulary does.

problemText: Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Zanzibar, and Sofala each had its own ruling family, minted or controlled its own commerce, and competed with the others for a share of the ocean trade. What political form does this describe?
choices: A single unified Swahili empire governed from Kilwa
Provinces of an Arabian caliphate administered from across the sea
Trading colonies founded and governed from Portugal
A chain of independent city-states, each consisting of a port and the territory around it
hints: Ask whether any one of these towns ever gave orders to the rest.

problemText: Archaeologists have excavated Chinese porcelain and Indian glass beads at Great Zimbabwe, a stone-walled inland capital several hundred miles from the coast that flourished from about 1100 to 1450 and controlled nearby goldfields. What does this evidence best show?
choices: Chinese merchants traveled inland in person to trade directly at Great Zimbabwe
Goods moved through a multi-stage relay — interior gold went out through the port of Sofala and the city-state of Kilwa, and Asian goods came back along the same chain
Great Zimbabwe was built by Chinese sailors who settled in southern Africa
The objects were dropped by Portuguese traders traveling inland after 1500
hints: Long-distance goods usually pass through many hands; ask whether any single traveler had to make the whole journey.

problemText: A Portuguese captain reported after reaching an East African harbor in the late 1490s (paraphrased): 'Here we found ships from Cambay in India and from Arabia loading cloth and spice, and pilots who knew the whole crossing to India by the stars.' Which conclusion is best supported by this account?
choices: Portuguese ships introduced long-distance navigation to the western Indian Ocean
The harbor's commerce had been organized by Chinese officials who were still stationed in the port
A well-established trading network with experienced navigators was already operating before the Portuguese arrived
East African ports had traded only with their immediate coastline until Europeans opened wider routes
hints: Focus on what the captain found already in place when he arrived, not on what he brought with him.

problemText: Chinese treasure fleets under the admiral Zheng He reached the Swahili coast between 1405 and 1433, after which the Ming court ended the voyages and dismantled the fleets. Portuguese ships arrived in 1498, and by 1505 were bombarding Kilwa and Mombasa and requiring other ships to buy passes. Which comparison of the two arrivals is most accurate?
choices: China withdrew because of a decision by its own government, while the Portuguese tried to control an existing network by force
Portuguese warships defeated the Chinese fleets and drove them out of the Indian Ocean
Both powers were repelled by a military alliance of the Swahili city-states
Both arrived as ordinary peaceful traders, and neither changed how commerce in the ocean worked
hints: Compare the cause behind each event: one is a policy choice made in a distant court, the other is a deliberate military strategy.
Check the dates before connecting them — the last treasure fleet came home in 1433, sixty-five years before any Portuguese ship reached this ocean.

problemText: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1345 on an island in a shallow lake, and by 1500 the city held roughly 200,000 people. What agricultural method did they build out into the lake bed to feed a city that size?
choices: Terraced stone hillsides fed by canals carrying meltwater from the mountains
Fenced pastures supporting large herds of cattle and sheep
Deeply plowed valley fields worked with iron plows
Chinampas — raised, highly fertile garden plots built up from the lake bed and harvested several times a year
hints: Three of these depend on animals or metals that did not exist in Mesoamerica before 1492 — and the Mexica engineered their site rather than finding a good one.

problemText: A carved monument at one Maya city records that its ruler was captured in battle by the ruler of a neighboring city. Both cities used the same script, the same calendar, and worshipped in the same religious tradition. What does this indicate about Classic Maya political organization, roughly 250 to 900?
choices: The Maya formed a single empire whose provinces occasionally rebelled against the capital
The Maya region was governed by outsiders who imposed a common script on it
The Maya shared one culture but were politically divided into many independent, rival kingdoms
Maya inscriptions are religious myth and record no real political events
hints: Shared writing and warfare between the writers are not a contradiction — ask what political unit lets both be true at the same time.

problemText: Maya scribes wrote numbers in a positional system built on a base of twenty that included a symbol for zero, and used it to track the solar year, a 260-day ritual calendar, and the cycles of Venus. What does this best demonstrate?
choices: The Maya learned place-value notation and the concept of zero from Indian mathematicians
The Maya developed place-value notation with zero on their own and applied it to precise astronomical timekeeping
Maya numerals could express quantities but were never used to record dates
The Maya counted in the same base of ten used around the Mediterranean
hints: Zero was invented more than once in human history; compare the counting base of each system before assuming one was copied.

problemText: After 1428 the Mexica and their allies conquered widely but generally left defeated city-states with their own rulers, gods, and soldiers, demanding only regular payments of cloth, cacao, food, labor, and captives. What was a predictable consequence of governing this way?
choices: Conquered peoples were steadily absorbed into Mexica identity and lost their own leadership
The empire was forced to station large permanent garrisons in every town it defeated
Subject peoples stayed organized and armed, so resentment could turn into rebellion or into alliance with an outside challenger
Tribute demands were so light that subject states barely noticed they were ruled at all
hints: Cheap rule buys its savings with a trade-off — ask what this system never took away from the peoples it defeated.

problemText: Between roughly 800 and 900, the great Maya cities of the southern lowlands stopped raising dated monuments and lost their populations, while northern centers such as Chichen Itza rose to prominence afterward; today about six to seven million Maya people live in Guatemala, southern Mexico, Belize, and Honduras. Which statement best describes what happened?
choices: A specific set of southern cities was abandoned amid drought, warfare, and strain on thin tropical soils, while Maya society continued elsewhere
The Maya people disappeared entirely and left no descendants
The Aztec Empire conquered the Maya and scattered the survivors
A single volcanic eruption destroyed every Maya settlement at once
hints: Ask precisely which places and which century the evidence covers — 'the civilization vanished' is a far larger claim than the record supports.

problemText: A student argues that Mesoamerican pyramids, writing, and the symbol for zero must have been taught to the Maya by visitors from Egypt or Asia. Which piece of evidence most directly undermines that argument?
choices: Some Mesoamerican pyramids cover a larger area at the base than Egyptian pyramids do
Maya glyphs share no signs or structure with Egyptian hieroglyphs, and Maya arithmetic runs on a base of twenty while Old World systems used ten or sixty
The Maya and the Egyptians lived in very different climates
Maya cities were built many centuries later than the Egyptian pyramids
hints: Similar problems can produce similar-looking solutions independently; look for details that a borrowed system would have had to carry along with it.
If one system had been copied from the other, the signs and the counting base would match — compare those two things directly.

problemText: The Inca ran a census of millions of people, tracked the contents of storehouses across their empire, and scheduled labor duties village by village — all without an alphabet. What device did their trained specialists use to hold this information?
choices: Clay tablets pressed with numerical marks and stored in Cusco
The quipu — bundles of dyed cords in which knot type and position encoded numbers
Carved stone tally pillars set at intervals along the royal roads
Painted bark-paper books kept by provincial governors
hints: The medium was fiber, not stone or paper — think of something light enough for a runner to carry over a mountain pass.

problemText: Under Inca rule, a village sends a rotation of households to build terraces, farm state fields, and serve in the army, and the state feeds and supplies those workers the entire time they serve. What is this obligation called?
choices: The mit'a — a tax paid in rotating labor rather than in goods
The encomienda — a Spanish grant giving colonists a claim on Indigenous labor
The mitmaq — the forced resettlement of whole communities far from their homeland
The chasqui — service as a relay messenger stationed along the royal roads
hints: Ask what actually changes hands: the village gives time and effort, and the state gives back food. One of these options is Spanish, not Inca.

problemText: The Inca built roughly 25,000 miles of engineered road with rope suspension bridges, stocked waystations, and relay runners — yet no carts ever ran on it. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Andean peoples had never encountered the idea of a wheel in any form
The Inca knew the wheel but had no draft animals to pull carts and terrain that favored stairways, so llamas and human porters carried the freight
Inca law forbade wheeled vehicles from traveling on the royal roads
The roads were deliberately built too narrow for anything wider than the ruler's litter
hints: A cart needs something to pull it — ask what large domesticated animals the Andes actually offered.

problemText: An Andean community under Inca rule holds maize fields in a warm valley, potato fields up near the frost line, and llama herds higher still — all at the same time. What problem does this arrangement solve?
choices: It exempted the community from owing labor service to the state
It concentrated all farming into one climate so that every harvest came in at the same time
It let the community raise cattle and sheep alongside its crops
It spread production across several climates at once, so a single frost or drought could not wipe out the whole food supply
hints: Andean geography stacks climates on top of one another — ask what holding several of them at once protects a village against.

problemText: Cahokia, on the Mississippi floodplain near present-day St. Louis, held roughly 10,000 to 20,000 people between about 1050 and 1350 and raised Monks Mound, the largest earthen structure in the Americas. What does this evidence best support?
choices: Parts of North America supported large, permanent settlements with enough organized labor to build monumental architecture
Every people of North America lived in cities of this size before 1492
Cahokia was built by Mesoamerican settlers who migrated north from the Valley of Mexico
Building in earth rather than stone shows that Cahokia's people had no lasting political organization
hints: Moving that much earth by hand takes planning, food surpluses, and many workers over many years — ask what that requires of a society.

problemText: The Inca governed roughly ten million people from Cusco using appointed officials, mandatory resettlement, and a labor tax. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy bound five nations under the Great Law of Peace: a shared council settled common matters by consensus while each nation ran its own internal affairs, and clan mothers chose and could remove the chiefs. Which comparison of the two is most accurate?
choices: Neither counts as real government, because neither one recorded its laws in writing
Both placed final authority in the hands of a single hereditary ruler
Both were durable political orders uniting many communities, but the Inca concentrated authority at the center while the Haudenosaunee distributed it among member nations
The Haudenosaunee modeled their council on Inca administration after contact between the two
hints: Both are answers to the same question — how do many communities act as one? — so ask where each of them puts the final say.
One commands from a center, the other negotiates among equals; neither the absence of writing nor the absence of a monarch means the absence of government.
